changes.before: Only one in a hundred machines has a fault. A model always says working. Is its high overall accuracy enough to trust fault detection?
changes.after: An overall score can hide the mistakes that matter most.

before: Evaluation compares a system’s behavior with clear expectations on relevant examples.
Accuracy counts the fraction of predictions that are correct. For example, nine correct out of ten means nine-tenths correct.

An overall score can hide an important kind of failure. If almost every message is ordinary, a system that calls every message ordinary can still have high accuracy while missing every urgent message.
Choose checks that reflect the task: which errors happen, who is affected, and what consequences follow.
Keep independent examples and compare the same task conditions when comparing systems. A good score on one benchmark does not establish performance on every task.
after: Evaluation checks results against clear expectations using examples that fit the intended task.
Accuracy is the share of predictions that are correct: correct predictions divided by all predictions.
If the task is to find urgent messages, missing all of them is a serious failure. Check which mistakes happen and what their effects are.
Compare systems on separate evaluation examples under the same task conditions. A good score on one test does not prove the model works well on every task.

before.question: Only one in a hundred machines has a fault. A model always says working. Is its high overall accuracy enough to trust fault detection?
choices: Yes. Overall accuracy proves every kind of case works.
Yes. Rare cases do not count as errors.
No. It misses every faulty machine despite many correct working labels.
before.explanation: The intended task makes missed faults important; a single aggregate score hides that failure.

after.question: Only 1 of 100 machines has a fault. A model always says working. Is its high accuracy enough to trust fault detection?
choices: Yes. Accuracy proves every kind of case works.
Yes. Rare cases do not count.
No. It misses the faulty machine.
after.explanation: The 99 working machines make accuracy look high. The model still fails to find the fault.
